01Chapter 1 · The Machine Learning Landscape

The Machine Learning Landscape

Machine learning ab science fiction nahi raha — billions log roz use karte hain. Spam filter 1990s mein pehla bada mainstream ML application tha, aur aaj voice prompts, automatic translation, image search, product recommendations aur chatbots tak har jagah ML hai. Yeh chapter ML ki basic definitions, uske types aur ek typical ML project ka workflow samjhata hai — bina zyada code ke, sirf concepts crystal clear karne ke liye.

Machine Learning kya hai?

Simple definition: machine learning woh science (aur art) hai jisme computers ko data se seekhne ke liye program kiya jata hai. Ek aur general definition kehti hai — ML woh field hai jo computers ko bina explicitly program kiye seekhne ki ability deta hai. Aur ek engineering wali definition: agar ek program experience E se, kisi task T par, performance measure P ke hisaab se behtar hota jaye, to woh seekh raha hai.

Spam filter iska best example hai: task T hai naye emails ko spam flag karna, experience E hai training data (spam aur ham emails ke examples), aur performance measure P ho sakta hai correctly classified emails ka ratio — jise accuracy kehte hain. Training ke liye use hone wale examples ko training set kehte hain, har example ko training instance ya sample, aur seekhne aur prediction karne wale hisse ko model kehte hain — jaise neural networks aur random forests.

Ek important baat: sirf Wikipedia download kar lene se computer ne kuch seekha nahi — jab tak woh kisi task par behtar na ho, woh machine learning nahi hai.

ML kyun use karein?

  • Lambi rule-lists se chutkara: traditional spam filter mein har pattern ke liye alag rule likhna padta tha — program lamba, mushkil aur maintain karna hard. ML model khud seekh leta hai kaunse words spam ke ache predictors hain, code chhota aur accurate hota hai.
  • Badalte environment mein adapt: spammers jab "4U" ki jagah "For U" likhne lage, to ML filter ne khud notice kiya ki "For U" spam mein frequent ho gaya hai, aur bina human intervention ke flag karne laga.
  • Complex problems: speech recognition jaise kaam — hazaaron words, lakhon log, noisy environment, kai languages — traditional rules se possible nahi. ML example recordings se khud seekhta hai.
  • Humans ko seekhne mein madad: trained model ko inspect karke pata chal sakta hai usne kya seekha — kabhi-kabhi unsuspected correlations ya naye trends dikh jate hain. Bade data mein hidden patterns dhoondhna data mining kehlata hai.

Applications ki jhalak

ML har jagah hai: production line par product images classify karna (image classification, CNNs ya vision transformers), brain scans mein tumors dhoondhna (semantic image segmentation — har pixel classify hota hai), news articles classify karna aur offensive comments flag karna (NLP / text classification), long documents summarize karna, DNA sequence se genetic risk estimate karna, chatbot banana, company revenue forecast karna (regression), voice commands samajhna (speech recognition), credit card fraud detect karna (anomaly detection), customers ko groups mein baantna (clustering), high-dimensional data ko diagram mein dikhana (dimensionality reduction), product recommend karna (recommender systems), aur games ke liye intelligent bot banana (reinforcement learning).

Yaad rakho: ML tab best hai jab (1) existing solution mein bahut mehnat aur maintenance lagti ho, (2) traditional approach se koi acha solution na milta ho, (3) environment badalta rehta ho, ya (4) complex problems aur bade data se insights nikalni hon.

python — Code example 1-1 — GitHub: https://github.com/ageron/handson-mlp/blob/main/01_the_machine_learning_landscape.ipynb
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Download and prepare the data
data_root = "https://github.com/ageron/data/raw/main/"
lifesat = pd.read_csv(data_root + "lifesat/lifesat.csv")
X = lifesat[["GDP per capita (USD)"]].values
y = lifesat[["Life satisfaction"]].values

# Visualize the data
lifesat.plot(kind='scatter', grid=True,
             x="GDP per capita (USD)", y="Life satisfaction")
plt.axis([23_500, 62_500, 4, 9])
plt.show()

# Select a linear model
model = LinearRegression()

# Train the model
model.fit(X, y)

# Make a prediction for Puerto Rico 
X_new = [[33_442.8]]  # Puerto Rico' GDP per capita in 2020
print(model.predict(X_new)) # outputs [[6.01610329]]

# Select a 3-Nearest Neighbors regression model
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3)

# Train the model
model.fit(X, y)

# Make a prediction for Puerto Rico
print(model.predict(X_new)) # outputs [[5.73333333]]

from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request

datapath = Path() / "datasets" / "lifesat"
datapath.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

data_root = "https://github.com/ageron/data/raw/main/"
for filename in ("oecd_bli.csv", "gdp_per_capita.csv"):
    if not (datapath / filename).is_file():
        print("Downloading", filename)
        url = data_root + "lifesat/" + filename
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, datapath / filename)

oecd_bli = pd.read_csv(datapath / "oecd_bli.csv")
gdp_per_capita = pd.read_csv(datapath / "gdp_per_capita.csv")

gdp_year = 2020
gdppc_col = "GDP per capita (USD)"
lifesat_col = "Life satisfaction"

gdp_per_capita = gdp_per_capita[gdp_per_capita["Year"] == gdp_year]
gdp_per_capita = gdp_per_capita.drop(["Code", "Year"], axis=1)
gdp_per_capita.columns = ["Country", gdppc_col]
gdp_per_capita.set_index("Country", inplace=True)

gdp_per_capita.head()

oecd_bli = oecd_bli[oecd_bli["INEQUALITY"]=="TOT"]
oecd_bli = oecd_bli.pivot(index="Country", columns="Indicator", values="Value")

oecd_bli.head()

full_country_stats = pd.merge(left=oecd_bli, right=gdp_per_capita,
                              left_index=True, right_index=True)
full_country_stats.sort_values(by=gdppc_col, inplace=True)
full_country_stats = full_country_stats[[gdppc_col, lifesat_col]]

full_country_stats.head()

min_gdp = 23_500
max_gdp = 62_500

country_stats = full_country_stats[(full_country_stats[gdppc_col] >= min_gdp) &
                                   (full_country_stats[gdppc_col] <= max_gdp)]
country_stats.head()

country_stats.to_csv(datapath / "lifesat.csv")
full_country_stats.to_csv(datapath / "lifesat_full.csv")

country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', figsize=(5, 3), grid=True,
                   x=gdppc_col, y=lifesat_col)

min_life_sat = 4
max_life_sat = 9

position_text = {
    "Turkey": (29_500, 4.2),
    "Hungary": (28_000, 6.9),
    "France": (40_000, 5),
    "New Zealand": (28_000, 8.2),
    "Australia": (50_000, 5.5),
    "United States": (59_000, 5.3),
    "Denmark": (46_000, 8.5)
}

for country, pos_text in position_text.items():
    pos_data_x = country_stats[gdppc_col].loc[country]
    pos_data_y = country_stats[lifesat_col].loc[country]
    country = "US" if country == "United States" else country
    plt.annotate(country, xy=(pos_data_x, pos_data_y),
                 xytext=pos_text, fontsize=12,
                 arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', width=0.5,
                                 shrink=0.08, headwidth=5))
    plt.plot(pos_data_x, pos_data_y, "ro")

plt.axis([min_gdp, max_gdp, min_life_sat, max_life_sat])

plt.show()

highlighted_countries = country_stats.loc[list(position_text.keys())]
highlighted_countries[[gdppc_col, lifesat_col]].sort_values(by=gdppc_col)

country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', figsize=(5, 3), grid=True,
                   x=gdppc_col, y=lifesat_col)

X = np.linspace(min_gdp, max_gdp, 1000)

w1, w2 = 4.2, 0
plt.plot(X, w1 + w2 * 1e-5 * X, "r")
plt.text(40_000, 4.9, fr"$\theta_0 = {w1}$", color="r")
plt.text(40_000, 4.4, fr"$\theta_1 = {w2}$", color="r")

w1, w2 = 10, -9
plt.plot(X, w1 + w2 * 1e-5 * X, "g")
plt.text(26_000, 8.5, fr"$\theta_0 = {w1}$", color="g")
plt.text(26_000, 8.0, fr"$\theta_1 = {w2} \times 10^{{-5}}$", color="g")

w1, w2 = 3, 8
plt.plot(X, w1 + w2 * 1e-5 * X, "b")
plt.text(48_000, 8.5, fr"$\theta_0 = {w1}$", color="b")
plt.text(48_000, 8.0, fr"$\theta_1 = {w2} \times 10^{{-5}}$", color="b")

plt.axis([min_gdp, max_gdp, min_life_sat, max_life_sat])

plt.show()

from sklearn import linear_model

X_sample = country_stats[[gdppc_col]].values

lin1 = linear_model.LinearRegression()

t0, t1 = lin1.intercept_[0], lin1.coef_[0][0]

country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', figsize=(5, 3), grid=True,

X = np.linspace(min_gdp, max_gdp, 1000)

plt.text(max_gdp - 20_000, min_life_sat + 1.9,

plt.text(max_gdp - 20_000, min_life_sat + 1.3,
         fr"$\theta_1 = {t1 * 1e5:.2f} \times 10^{{-5}}$", color="b")

plt.axis([min_gdp, max_gdp, min_life_sat, max_life_sat])

puerto_rico_gdp_per_capita

puerto_rico_predicted_life_satisfaction

country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', figsize=(5, 3), grid=True,

plt.text(min_gdp + 22_000, max_life_sat - 1.1,

plt.plot([puerto_rico_gdp_per_capita, puerto_rico_gdp_per_capita],
         [min_life_sat, puerto_rico_predicted_life_satisfaction], "r--")
plt.text(puerto_rico_gdp_per_capita + 1000, 5.0,

         color="r")
plt.plot(puerto_rico_gdp_per_capita, puerto_rico_predicted_life_satisfaction,
         "ro")

plt.axis([min_gdp, max_gdp, min_life_sat, max_life_sat])

plt.show()

missing_data = full_country_stats[(full_country_stats[gdppc_col] < min_gdp) |
                                  (full_country_stats[gdppc_col] > max_gdp)]
missing_data

position_text_missing_countries = {
    "South Africa": (20_000, 4.2),
    "Colombia": (6_000, 8.2),
    "Brazil": (18_000, 7.8),
    "Mexico": (24_000, 7.4),
    "Chile": (30_000, 7.0),
    "Norway": (51_000, 6.2),
    "Switzerland": (62_000, 5.7),
    "Ireland": (81_000, 5.2),
    "Luxembourg": (92_000, 4.7),
}

full_country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', figsize=(8, 3),
                        x=gdppc_col, y=lifesat_col, grid=True)

for country, pos_text in position_text_missing_countries.items():
    pos_data_x, pos_data_y = missing_data.loc[country]
    plt.annotate(country, xy=(pos_data_x, pos_data_y),
                 xytext=pos_text, fontsize=12,
                 arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', width=0.5,
                                 shrink=0.08, headwidth=5))
    plt.plot(pos_data_x, pos_data_y, "rs")

X = np.linspace(0, 115_000, 1000)
plt.plot(X, t0 + t1 * X, "b:")

lin_reg_full = linear_model.LinearRegression()
Xfull = np.c_[full_country_stats[gdppc_col]]
yfull = np.c_[full_country_stats[lifesat_col]]
lin_reg_full.fit(Xfull, yfull)

t0full, t1full = lin_reg_full.intercept_[0], lin_reg_full.coef_[0][0]
X = np.linspace(0, 115_000, 1000)
plt.plot(X, t0full + t1full * X, "k")

plt.axis([0, 115_000, min_life_sat, max_life_sat])

plt.show()

from sklearn import preprocessing
from sklearn import pipeline

full_country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', figsize=(8, 3),
                        x=gdppc_col, y=lifesat_col, grid=True)

w_countries = [c for c in full_country_stats.index if "W" in c.upper()]
full_country_stats.loc[w_countries][lifesat_col]

all_w_countries = [c for c in gdp_per_capita.index if "W" in c.upper()]
gdp_per_capita.loc[all_w_countries].sort_values(by=gdppc_col)

country_stats.plot(kind='scatter', x=gdppc_col, y=lifesat_col, figsize=(8, 3))
missing_data.plot(kind='scatter', x=gdppc_col, y=lifesat_col,

X = np.linspace(0, 115_000, 1000)
plt.plot(X, t0 + t1*X, "b:", label="Linear model on partial data")
plt.plot(X, t0full + t1full * X, "k-", label="Linear model on all data")

ridge = linear_model.Ridge(alpha=10**9.5)
X_sample = country_stats[[gdppc_col]]
y_sample = country_stats[[lifesat_col]]
ridge.fit(X_sample, y_sample)
t0ridge, t1ridge = ridge.intercept_[0], ridge.coef_[0]
plt.plot(X, t0ridge + t1ridge * X, "b--",
         label="Regularized linear model on partial data")
plt.legend(loc="lower right")

plt.axis([0, 115_000, min_life_sat, max_life_sat])

plt.show()

01.1Chapter 1 · The Machine Learning Landscape

ML Systems ke Types — Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, Self-supervised, Reinforcement

ML systems ko teen criteria se classify kiya jata hai: training mein kitni supervision milti hai, kya system on-the-fly seekh sakta hai, aur woh generalize kaise karta hai — examples yaad karke ya model banakar. Yeh criteria exclusive nahi hain — ek hi system online, model-based aur supervised ho sakta hai, jaise ek modern spam filter.

Supervised learning — labels ke saath seekhna

Supervised learning mein training set mein desired solutions bhi hote hain, jinhe labels kehte hain. Iske do sabse common tasks hain: classification — jaise spam ya ham classify karna — aur regression — jaise car ki mileage, age aur brand se uski price predict karna. Target aur label aksar synonyms hain — regression mein "target" zyada common hai, classification mein "label". Features ko kabhi-kabhi predictors ya attributes bhi kehte hain. Dhyaan do: kuch regression models classification ke liye bhi use ho sakte hain — jaise logistic regression kisi class ki probability output karta hai.

Unsupervised learning — bina teacher ke

  • Clustering: blog visitors ko similar groups mein baantna — jaise 40% teenagers jo comics pasand karte hain, 20% adults jo sci-fi pasand karte hain. Algorithm ko kabhi bataya nahi jata kaun kis group mein hai.
  • Visualization aur dimensionality reduction: complex unlabeled data ko 2D/3D mein plot karna, ya correlated features ko merge karke data simplify karna — jaise car ki mileage aur age ko milakar "wear and tear" ka ek feature banana. Yeh feature extraction hai. Dimensionality reduce karne se model fast chalta hai, kam memory lagti hai, aur kabhi performance bhi behtar hoti hai.
  • Anomaly detection: unusual credit card transactions ya manufacturing defects pakadna — system mostly normal instances dekhkar seekhta hai, phir naye instance ko normal ya anomaly batata hai. Novelty detection isse milta-julta hai, par isme training set bilkul clean hona chahiye.
  • Association rule learning: bade data mein attributes ke beech interesting relations dhoondhna — jaise supermarket mein barbecue sauce aur potato chips khareedne wale steak bhi lete hain.

Semi-supervised aur self-supervised learning

Data label karna time-consuming aur costly hota hai, isliye aksar bahut saare unlabeled instances aur thode se labeled instances hote hain. Semi-supervised learning partially labeled data se kaam karta hai — jaise photo service pehle clustering se pehchan leti hai ki kaunsa shakhs kis photos mein hai, phir aap ek label de do to woh har photo mein naam laga deti hai. Self-supervised learning mein fully unlabeled data se fully labeled dataset generate kiya jata hai — jaise image ka ek chhota hissa mask karke model ko original image recover karna sikhana. Phir is model ko fine-tune karke asli task — jaise pet species classify karna — sikhaya jata hai. Ek task se doosre task mein knowledge transfer karna transfer learning kehlata hai, aur yeh aaj ki sabse important techniques mein se ek hai. Bade language models bhi isi tarah train hote hain — text mein random words mask karke missing words predict karna sikhaya jata hai.

Reinforcement learning — agent, environment aur reward

Reinforcement learning bilkul alag hai: yahan agent environment ko observe karta hai, actions leta hai, aur badle mein rewards (ya negative rewards = penalties) pata hai. Use khud best strategy — jise policy kehte hain — seekhni hoti hai, jo time ke saath sabse zyada reward de. Robots chalna seekhna aur game-playing programs iske examples hain. Ek mashhoor game-playing program ne lakhon games analyze karke aur khud se khelkar apni winning policy seekhi thi — lekin champion ke against khelte waqt learning band thi, sirf seekhi hui policy apply ho rahi thi (offline learning).

Yaad rakho: supervised = labeled data (classification, regression); unsupervised = unlabeled data (clustering, visualization, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, association rules); semi-supervised = thoda labeled + bahut unlabeled; self-supervised = unlabeled se labels generate karke; reinforcement = reward se policy seekhna.
SOURCESource: Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — The Machine Learning Landscape

01.2Chapter 1 · The Machine Learning Landscape

Batch vs Online, Instance-Based vs Model-Based, aur ML Project Workflow

Supervision ke alawa ML systems ko do aur tareekon se classify kiya jata hai — kya woh incremental seekh sakte hain, aur woh generalize kaise karte hain. Inhi concepts se ek typical ML project ka workflow banta hai, jo is section mein ek real example — life satisfaction aur GDP — se samjhaya gaya hai.

Batch vs online learning

Batch learning mein system ko saara available data ek saath dekar train kiya jata hai — yeh generally offline hota hai, time aur computing resources bahut lagte hain, aur train hone ke baad model aur seekhta nahi, sirf apply karta hai. Problem yeh hai ki duniya badalti rehti hai aur model purana pad jata hai — is phenomenon ko data drift ya model rot kehte hain. Solution hai model ko regularly naye data par dobara train karna — roz ya hafte mein ek baar. Lekin poora data dobara train karna mehenga ho sakta hai, aur huge data ya limited resources (jaise smartphone app) mein impossible bhi.

Online learning mein system ko data instances ek-ek karke ya chhote groups (mini-batches) mein incrementally train kiya jata hai — har step fast aur cheap hota hai, isliye system naye data se on-the-fly seekh sakta hai. Yeh rapidly changing data (jaise stock market) aur huge datasets ke liye best hai jo ek machine ki memory mein fit nahi hote — isse out-of-core learning kehte hain. Important parameter hai learning rate: zyada rate par system naye data se jaldi adapt karta hai par purana bhool jata hai (catastrophic forgetting), kam rate par seekhna slow hota hai par noise se kam affect hota hai. Online learning ka bada risk: agar kharab data feed ho gaya (bug ya koi system ko game karne ki koshish), to performance jaldi gir sakti hai — isliye monitor karna aur zaroorat par learning band karke purane state par wapas jana zaroori hai.

Instance-based vs model-based learning

Instance-based learning mein system examples ko yaad kar leta hai aur naye case ko similarity measure se compare karke generalize karta hai — jaise naye email ko spam flag karna agar usme known spam emails se bahut saare common words hon. Yeh chhote aur badalte datasets mein acha hai, par scale nahi karta: production mein poora training set deploy karna padta hai, prediction slow hoti hai, aur high-dimensional data (jaise images) mein acha kaam nahi karta.

Model-based learning mein examples se ek model banaya jata hai aur phir us model se predictions ki jati hain. Example: life satisfaction ko GDP per capita ka linear function mana gaya — life_satisfaction = θ0 + θ1 × GDP_per_capita. Yeh step model selection hai. Phir ek cost function (ya loss function) define ki jati hai jo batati hai model kitna kharab hai — linear regression mein typically predictions aur training examples ke beech ki distance — aur training algorithm woh parameters dhoondhta hai jo is cost ko minimize karein. Is example mein best values mili: θ0 = 3.75 aur θ1 = 6.78 × 10⁻⁵. Phir prediction: GDP per capita $33,442 wale region ki life satisfaction lagbhag 3.75 + 33,442 × 6.78 × 10⁻⁵ = 6.02. Instance-based tareeke (3 nearest neighbors) se isi case mein 5.73 milta — thoda alag answer.

Typical ML workflow — chaar steps

  • Data study karo: data ko dekho, samjho, plot karo.
  • Model select karo: model ka type aur architecture choose karo — "model" word ke teen matlab hote hain: model ka type, fully specified architecture, ya final trained model.
  • Model train karo: learning algorithm cost function minimize karne wale parameter values dhoondhta hai. Model ke parameters (jaise θ0, θ1) training se seekhe jate hain — hyperparameters se alag, jo training se pehle set kiye jate hain aur training ke dauraan constant rehte hain.
  • Predictions karo (inference): trained model ko naye cases par apply karo, umeed hai ki woh generalize karega.

Iske alawa bhi categories hain: ensemble learning (multiple models train karke unki predictions combine karna), federated learning (multiple devices par raw data share kiye bina train karna — privacy ke liye), aur meta-learning (seekhna kaise seekhna hai — kam data se naye tasks jaldi seekhna).

Yaad rakho: batch = poora data ek saath, offline, dobara train karna padta hai; online = incremental, mini-batches, out-of-core possible, learning rate balance zaroori; instance-based = examples yaad + similarity; model-based = model banao + parameters fit karo + inference karo.
SOURCESource: Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — The Machine Learning Landscape

01.3Chapter 1 · The Machine Learning Landscape

ML ki Challenges — Data, Overfitting, Testing aur Fine-tuning

ML project mein do cheezein galat ho sakti hain — "bad model" aur "bad data". Data ki problems, overfitting/underfitting, aur sahi testing ka tareeka samajhna hi ek ache ML system aur kharab system ka farq hai.

Bad data — quantity, representativeness, quality, relevance

  • Insufficient quantity: bachcha ek-do baar mein apple pehchan leta hai, ML nahi — simple problems mein hazaaron examples chahiye, image ya speech recognition mein lakhon. Ek mashhoor paper ne dikhaya ki kaafi data milne par bahut alag-alag algorithms bhi lagbhag ek jaisa perform karte hain — data algorithms se zyada matter kar sakta hai.
  • Nonrepresentative data: training data un cases ko represent karna chahiye jin par generalize karna hai. Life satisfaction example mein GDP $23,500 se kam ya $62,500 se zyada wale countries hi nahi the — unhe add karte hi model badal gaya aur pata chala linear model kabhi acha kaam nahi karega. Chhota sample ho ya flawed sampling method — dono se sampling bias hota hai. 1936 ke ek bade chunav mein ek bahut bade poll (lagbhag 10 million logon ko bheja, 2.4 million jawab) ne galat winner predict kiya tha — kyunki addresses ameer logon ki lists se liye gaye the aur 25% se kam logon ne jawab diya tha (nonresponse bias).
  • Poor-quality data: errors, outliers aur noise patterns dhoondhna mushkil kar dete hain. Outliers ko discard ya fix karo; missing features (jaise 5% customers ne age nahi batayi) ko ignore karo, un instances ko hatao, ya median jaisi value se bharo.
  • Irrelevant features: garbage in, garbage out. Ache features banana — feature engineering — critical hai: feature selection (sabse useful features chunna), feature extraction (existing features combine karke behtar feature banana), aur naye data se naye features create karna.

Overfitting aur underfitting

Overfitting matlab model training data par bahut acha perform karta hai par naye instances par generalize nahi karta — jaise high-degree polynomial model jo training points ke aas-paas wiggle karta hai. Complex model noisy ya chhote training set mein noise ke patterns bhi seekh leta hai — jaise sirf isliye ki training mein "w" wale naam ke countries ki life satisfaction 7 se zyada thi, model "w-satisfaction rule" bana le. Solutions: model simplify karo (kam parameters, kam attributes, ya constrain karo), zyada training data lao, ya noise kam karo. Model ko constrain karke simple banana regularization kehlata hai — regularization hyperparameter se control hota hai ki kitna constrain karna hai. Zyada regularization se model almost flat ho jata hai aur acha solution nahi milta; kam se overfitting rehta hai — sahi balance chahiye.

Underfitting iska ulta hai — model bahut simple hai aur data ki underlying structure seekh hi nahi pata, jaise life satisfaction ke liye linear model. Fix: zyada powerful model lo, behtar features do (feature engineering), ya model par constraints kam karo.

Testing aur validation — test set ko kabhi chhedo mat

Generalization error (out-of-sample error) jaanne ka ek tareeka hai data ko training set aur test set mein baantna — aam taur par 80% training, 20% testing. Training error kam aur generalization error zyada ho to overfitting hai. Lekin dhyaan: agar tum test set par hyperparameters tune karoge, to model usi test set ke liye fit ho jayega aur naye data par utna acha nahi karega. Solution hai holdout validation: training set ka ek hissa validation set (ya dev set) ke roop mein alag rakho, candidate models ko reduced training set par train karke validation set par compare karo, best model ko phir full training set par train karo, aur aakhir mein test set par evaluate karo. Agar validation set bahut chhota ho to evaluation galat ho sakti hai, bahut bada ho to training set chhota pad jata hai — isliye repeated cross-validation use hoti hai: kai chhote validation sets, har model har set par ek baar evaluate hota hai, aur average liya jata hai (training time badh jata hai, yeh drawback hai).

Data mismatch aur No Free Lunch

Kabhi training data production data ko perfectly represent nahi karta — jaise web se lakhon flower photos mil jayengi, par mobile app se li gayi sirf 1,000 representative photos hongi. Rule: validation aur test set hamesha production jaisi representative data se bane hon. Overfitting aur data mismatch ko alag karne ke liye ek aur set use hota hai — train-dev set: training data ka ek hissa alag rakho. Agar model train-dev par kharab hai, to overfitting hai (model simplify karo, zyada data lao, data clean karo). Agar train-dev par acha hai par dev set par kharab, to data mismatch hai (web images ko mobile photos jaisa banane ke liye preprocess karo aur dobara train karo). Aakhir mein — No Free Lunch theorem: agar data ke baare mein bilkul koi assumption na ho, to koi bhi model doosre se a priori behtar nahi hai. Kisi dataset ke liye linear model best hai, kisi ke liye neural network — kaunsa best hai, yeh sirf evaluate karke pata chalta hai. Isliye reasonable assumptions banao aur kuch reasonable models evaluate karo.

Yaad rakho: deployment mein bhi issues aate hain — model bahut complex, bahut bada, bahut slow, ya outdated ho sakta hai. Isliye companies mein alag MLOps team hoti hai. Aur test set ko sirf aakhir mein use karo — uspar tuning karna cheating jaisa hai, estimate optimistic ho jata hai.
SOURCESource: Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — The Machine Learning Landscape

02Chapter 2 · End-to-End Machine Learning Projects

End-to-End Machine Learning Project

Is chapter mein tum ek real estate company mein naye hire hue data scientist ban kar ek poora ML project end-to-end karoge — California census data se district ki median housing price predict karna. Example fictitious hai, goal real estate seekhna nahi, balki ek ML project ke main steps dikhana hai.

Project ke 8 steps

  • 1. Big picture dekho: problem frame karo, business objective samjho.
  • 2. Data lo: data download karo aur load karo.
  • 3. Explore aur visualize karo: insights gain karo.
  • 4. Data prepare karo: ML algorithms ke liye data taiyaar karo.
  • 5. Model select karo aur train karo.
  • 6. Model fine-tune karo.
  • 7. Solution present karo.
  • 8. Launch, monitor aur maintain karo.

Seekhte waqt real-world data use karna best hai — open datasets ke sources: Google Datasets Search, Hugging Face Datasets, OpenML, Kaggle, PapersWithCode, UC Irvine ML Repository, aur bhi kai. Is chapter mein California Housing Prices dataset use hota hai — 1990 California census par based, har district ke liye population, median income aur median housing price jaise metrics. District matlab block group — Census Bureau ki sabse chhoti geographical unit, typically 600 se 3,000 log.

Problem frame karna

Pehla sawaal: business objective kya hai? Model ka output (district ki median housing price ka prediction) ek aur ML system ko feed hoga, jo decide karega ki kisi area mein invest karna worth hai ya nahi — isliye accuracy bahut important hai. Current solution: experts manually estimate karte hain — costly, time-consuming, aur aksar 30% se zyada galat. Yeh supervised learning task hai (har instance ke saath expected output hai), regression task hai (value predict karni hai), multiple regression (multiple features use honge) aur univariate regression (sirf ek value predict karni hai). Data chhota hai, memory mein fit hota hai, continuous flow nahi hai — isliye plain batch learning kaafi hai. Agar data huge hota to multiple servers par split karke ya online learning use karte.

Performance measure — RMSE vs MAE

Regression ke liye typical performance measure hai root mean squared error (RMSE) — yeh batata hai predictions mein typically kitni error hoti hai, aur badi errors ko zyada weight deta hai. Notations: m = instances ki sankhya, x(i) = ith instance ka feature vector, y(i) = uska label, X = saare features ki matrix (har row ek instance), h = prediction function (hypothesis), ŷ(i) = h(x(i)) = predicted value. Agar bahut outliers hon to RMSE sensitive hota hai — tab mean absolute error (MAE) behtar ho sakta hai. Dono hi norms hain: RMSE Euclidean norm (ℓ2) se, MAE Manhattan norm (ℓ1) se related hai. Norm index jitna bada, utna zyada focus badi values par — isliye RMSE outliers se zyada affect hota hai, par bell-shaped data mein bahut acha perform karta hai.

Assumptions check karna

Kaam shuru karne se pehle assumptions list karo aur verify karo — serious issues early pakde jate hain. Example: agar downstream system prices ko categories (cheap/medium/expensive) mein convert karke use karta, to problem classification hoti, regression nahi — aur yeh baat months ka kaam karne ke baad pata chalti to bahut nuksaan hota. Is project mein downstream team ne confirm kiya ki unhe actual prices chahiye — lights green hain, coding shuru karo!

Yaad rakho: pehle business objective samjho, phir problem frame karo (supervised/unsupervised, classification/regression, batch/online), phir performance measure chuno, aur assumptions verify karo — coding uske baad.

02.1Chapter 2 · End-to-End Machine Learning Projects

Data Lena aur Explore Karna — California Housing

Code examples Jupyter notebooks mein hain, jo Google Colab par free mein online run hote hain — kuch install kiye bina. Notebook cells se bane hote hain (code ya text), Shift-Enter se run hote hain, aur code runtime par chalta hai, tumhari machine par nahi. Data lene, dekhne aur test set banane ka kaam yahan detail mein hai.

Data download aur pehli jhalak

Data ek compressed file housing.tgz mein hai, jisme housing.csv hai. Manual download ki jagah ek function likhna behtar hai — data regularly change ho to script se fresh data fetch ho sakta hai, aur multiple machines par install karna easy hota hai. Dataset mein 20,640 instances hain aur 10 attributes: longitude, latitude, housing_median_age, total_rooms, total_bedrooms, population, households, median_income, median_house_value, ocean_proximity. total_bedrooms mein sirf 20,433 non-null values hain — 207 districts mein yeh feature missing hai, baad mein handle karna padega. ocean_proximity ek categorical attribute hai — categories: <1H OCEAN (9,136), INLAND (6,551), NEAR OCEAN (2,658), NEAR BAY (2,290), ISLAND (sirf 5).

describe() se summary milta hai — count, mean, std (standard deviation — values kitni dispersed hain), min, max, aur percentiles (25%, 50% median, 75%). Histograms se pata chala: median income USD mein nahi hai — scaled aur capped hai (15 par upar, 0.5 par neeche; 3 ka matlab lagbhag $30,000), median house value bhi capped hai ($500,000) — yeh target attribute hai, isliye serious problem ho sakti hai; attributes ke scales bahut alag hain; aur kai histograms right-skewed hain.

Test set banao — pehle, aur phir use dekho mat

Data ko aur explore karne se pehle test set banao, side mein rakho, aur kabhi dekho mat — warna data snooping bias hota hai: tumhara dimaag test data mein pattern dekh lega, tum us hisaab se model chun loge, aur generalization error ka estimate bahut optimistic ho jayega. Typically 20% data test set mein jata hai. Random split mein problem: program dobara run karo to alag test set ban jata hai. Solutions: test set save karke rakhna, random seed fix karna (jaise random_state=42), ya har instance ke stable identifier ka hash use karna — jaise latitude + longitude se bana ID, jo lakhon saal stable rehta hai. Scikit-Learn ka train_test_split() sabse easy tareeka hai.

Purely random sampling hamesha kaafi nahi hoti — chhote dataset mein sampling bias aa sakta hai. Stratified sampling mein population ko homogeneous subgroups (strata) mein baanta jata hai aur har stratum se sahi proportion mein sample liya jata hai — jaise survey mein 51.1% females ka ratio maintain karna. Yahan median income important attribute hai, isliye usse 5 income categories banayi gayi (pd.cut() se, bins 0–1.5–3–4.5–6–infinity) aur StratifiedShuffleSplit ya train_test_split(..., stratify=...) se stratified split kiya gaya — stratified test set ke income proportions full dataset jaisi hi nikli, jabki random test set skewed thi.

Explore aur visualize — correlations aur naye features

Geographical scatterplot (alpha 0.2 se density dikhti hai) mein Bay Area, Los Angeles, San Diego aur Central Valley (Sacramento, Fresno) mein high density dikhi. Price map mein dikha ki prices location aur population density se strongly related hain — ocean ke paas mehenga. Correlation coefficient (Pearson's r) –1 se 1 tak hota hai: median income ka median house value se correlation 0.688 — sabse strong. Latitude ka –0.14 (uttar jaate hue prices thode kam). Lekin correlation sirf linear relationships measure karta hai — nonlinear relationships ko miss kar sakta hai (correlation 0 hone par bhi axes independent nahi hote).

Naye combined features try karo: rooms_per_house = total_rooms / households, bedrooms_ratio = total_bedrooms / total_rooms, people_per_house = population / households. Result: bedrooms_ratio ka correlation -0.256 — bahut behtar, aur negative: kam bedroom/room ratio wale ghar zyada mehenge lagte hain. Dhyaan: naye features banate waqt existing features se bahut linearly correlated features mat banao — collinearity linear regression jaise models mein problem karti hai.

Yaad rakho: explore karne se pehle test set alag karo. Stratified sampling tab use karo jab koi attribute bahut important ho. Correlation dekhna shuruaat hai — naye combined features aksar zyada informative hote hain.

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import tarfile
import urllib.request

def load_housing_data():
    tarball_path = Path("datasets/housing.tgz")
    if not tarball_path.is_file():
        Path("datasets").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        url = "https://github.com/ageron/data/raw/main/housing.tgz"
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, tarball_path)
        with tarfile.open(tarball_path) as housing_tarball:
            housing_tarball.extractall(path="datasets", filter="data")
    return pd.read_csv(Path("datasets/housing/housing.csv"))

housing_full = load_housing_data()

python — Test set banana — GitHub: https://github.com/ageron/handson-mlp/blob/main/02_end_to_end_machine_learning_project.ipynb
import numpy as np

def shuffle_and_split_data(data, test_ratio, rng):
    shuffled_indices = rng.permutation(len(data))
    test_set_size = int(len(data) * test_ratio)
    test_indices = shuffled_indices[:test_set_size]
    train_indices = shuffled_indices[test_set_size:]
    return data.iloc[train_indices], data.iloc[test_indices]

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
train_set, test_set = shuffle_and_split_data(housing_full, 0.2, rng)
len(train_set)

len(test_set)

from zlib import crc32

def is_id_in_test_set(identifier, test_ratio):
    return crc32(np.int64(identifier)) < test_ratio * 2**32

def split_data_with_id_hash(data, test_ratio, id_column):
    ids = data[id_column]
    in_test_set = ids.apply(lambda id_: is_id_in_test_set(id_, test_ratio))
    return data.loc[~in_test_set], data.loc[in_test_set]

housing_with_id = housing_full.reset_index()  # adds an `index` column
train_set, test_set = split_data_with_id_hash(housing_with_id, 0.2, "index")

housing_with_id["id"] = (housing_full["longitude"] * 1000
                         + housing_full["latitude"])
train_set, test_set = split_data_with_id_hash(housing_with_id, 0.2, "id")

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train_set, test_set = train_test_split(housing_full, test_size=0.2,
                                       random_state=42)

test_set["total_bedrooms"].isnull().sum()

# extra code – shows how to compute the 10.7% proba of getting a bad sample

from scipy.stats import binom

sample_size = 1000
ratio_female = 0.516
proba_too_small = binom(sample_size, ratio_female).cdf(490 - 1)
proba_too_large = 1 - binom(sample_size, ratio_female).cdf(540)
print(proba_too_small + proba_too_large)

# extra code – shows another way to estimate the probability of bad sample

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
samples = (rng.random((100_000, sample_size)) < ratio_female).sum(axis=1)
((samples < 490) | (samples > 540)).mean()

housing_full["income_cat"] = pd.cut(housing_full["median_income"],
                                    bins=[0., 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6., np.inf],
                                    labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

cat_counts = housing_full["income_cat"].value_counts().sort_index()
cat_counts.plot.bar(rot=0, grid=True)
plt.xlabel("Income category")
plt.ylabel("Number of districts")

plt.show()

from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedShuffleSplit

splitter = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=10, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
strat_splits = []
for train_index, test_index in splitter.split(housing_full,
                                              housing_full["income_cat"]):
    strat_train_set_n = housing_full.iloc[train_index]
    strat_test_set_n = housing_full.iloc[test_index]
    strat_splits.append([strat_train_set_n, strat_test_set_n])

strat_train_set, strat_test_set = strat_splits[0]

strat_train_set, strat_test_set = train_test_split(
    housing_full, test_size=0.2, stratify=housing_full["income_cat"],
    random_state=42)

strat_test_set["income_cat"].value_counts() / len(strat_test_set)

# extra code – computes the data for Figure 2–10

def income_cat_proportions(data):
    return data["income_cat"].value_counts() / len(data)

train_set, test_set = train_test_split(housing_full, test_size=0.2,
                                       random_state=42)

compare_props = pd.DataFrame({
    "Overall %": income_cat_proportions(housing_full),
    "Stratified %": income_cat_proportions(strat_test_set),
    "Random %": income_cat_proportions(test_set),
}).sort_index()
compare_props.index.name = "Income Category"
compare_props["Strat. Error %"] = (compare_props["Stratified %"] /
                                   compare_props["Overall %"] - 1)
compare_props["Rand. Error %"] = (compare_props["Random %"] /
                                  compare_props["Overall %"] - 1)
(compare_props * 100).round(2)

for set_ in (strat_train_set, strat_test_set):
    set_.drop("income_cat", axis=1, inplace=True)

02.2Chapter 2 · End-to-End Machine Learning Projects

Data Prepare Karna — Cleaning, Features, Scaling

Data preparation mein zyada kaam functions likhkar karna chahiye — taaki transformations reproduce ho sakein, reuse ho sakein, live system mein naye data par apply ho sakein, aur alag-alag combinations try karke best wali chunni ja sake. Pehle predictors aur labels alag karo — dono par same transformations nahi lagte.

Missing values clean karna — imputation

Zyada ML algorithms missing features ke saath kaam nahi kar sakte. total_bedrooms ke missing values ke liye teen options: (1) woh districts hata do, (2) poora attribute hata do, (3) missing values ko kisi value se bhar do — isse imputation kehte hain. Yahan option 3 chuna gaya, SimpleImputer(strategy="median") se. Imputer ka fayda: woh median values store kar leta hai (statistics_ mein), isliye training set ke saath-saath validation set, test set aur naye data par bhi same medians use ho sakte hain. Missing values ko mean (strategy="mean"), most frequent value, ya constant se bhi bhara ja sakta hai. Aur powerful imputers bhi hain: KNNImputer (k-nearest neighbors ke values ka mean) aur IterativeImputer (har feature ke liye regression model train karke missing values predict karna, kai iterations tak).

Scikit-Learn design — estimators, transformers, predictors

Scikit-Learn API ke main principles: consistency — sab objects ka interface same hai; estimators — jo dataset se parameters estimate karte hain, estimation fit() se hoti hai, hyperparameters constructor se set hote hain; transformers — estimators jo dataset transform karte hain (transform(), aur fit_transform() dono ek saath); predictors — jo predictions karte hain (predict() aur score() methods). Inspection — hyperparameters public instance variables hain (jaise imputer.strategy), learned parameters underscore suffix ke saath (jaise imputer.statistics_). Composition — building blocks reuse hote hain, jaise Pipeline. Sensible defaults — zyada parameters ke reasonable defaults hote hain, jaldi baseline ban jata hai. Transformers ka output NumPy array hota hai (column names nahi) — DataFrame wapas banane ke liye columns aur index recover karne padte hain, ya get_feature_names_out() use karo.

Categorical attributes — ordinal vs one-hot encoding

ocean_proximity text hai par limited categories hain — yeh categorical attribute hai. OrdinalEncoder categories ko numbers mein convert karta hai (jaise INLAND → 1, NEAR BAY → 3), par problem: ML algorithms maan lete hain ki paas wale numbers zyada similar hain — ocean proximity ke liye yeh galat hai. Solution hai one-hot encoding: har category ke liye ek binary attribute (1 jab woh category ho, 0 warna) — OneHotEncoder se. Output by default sparse matrix hota hai (mostly zeros wali matrix ke liye memory-efficient), sparse_output=False se dense array milta hai. Pandas ka get_dummies() bhi one-hot karta hai, par woh training categories yaad nahi rakhta — production mein nayi category aaye to woh naya column bana dega, jabki OneHotEncoder unknown category par exception deta hai (ya handle_unknown="ignore" se zeros deta hai). Bahut zyada categories hon to one-hot se features bahut badh jate hain — tab categories ko useful numerical features se replace karo (jaise ocean proximity → ocean se distance) ya neural networks mein embeddings use karo.

Feature scaling aur transformation

  • Min-max scaling (MinMaxScaler): values ko 0–1 range mein laata hai (ya feature_range se koi aur range, jaise neural networks ke liye –1 se 1). Outliers se bahut affect hota hai.
  • Standardization (StandardScaler): mean subtract karke standard deviation se divide karta hai — mean 0, standard deviation 1. Kisi specific range mein restrict nahi karta aur outliers se kam affect hota hai.
  • Heavy tail: agar feature ki distribution mein lambi tail hai, to pehle transform karo — positive right-tail feature ka square root ya logarithm lo (population feature log lene par lagbhag Gaussian/bell-shaped ho gaya). Bucketizing bhi option hai — distribution ko equal-sized buckets mein baantna.
  • Multimodal distribution: jaise housing_median_age mein kai peaks hain — bucketize karke buckets ko categories ki tarah one-hot karo, ya har mode ke liye Gaussian RBF similarity feature banao (exp(-γ(x-35)²) — 35 ke aas-paas peak hota hai).
  • Target transform: agar target ki heavy tail ho to uska log lo, par prediction ko wapas exponential se convert karna padega — TransformedTargetRegressor yeh automatically karta hai, aur transformers ka inverse_transform() bhi madad karta hai.

Warning: scalers ko sirf training data par fit karo — kabhi validation ya test set par fit() mat karo. Trained scaler se phir kisi bhi set ko transform() kar sakte ho.

Custom transformers aur pipelines

Apne transformers bhi likh sakte ho: bina training wale ke liye FunctionTransformer (jaise log transform, RBF similarity, ya ratio features — jaise column_ratio jo do features ka ratio nikalta hai). Trainable custom transformer ke liye class likho jisme fit() (hamesha self return kare), transform() aur fit_transform() hon — TransformerMixin se fit_transform() free milta hai, BaseEstimator se get_params()/set_params(). Example: ClusterSimilarity transformer — KMeans se 10 cluster centers dhoondhta hai (labels se weighted, taaki expensive districts par focus rahe) aur har district ki har cluster center se Gaussian RBF similarity nikalta hai. Pipeline se steps ko sequence mein chalaya jata hai (impute → scale), aur ColumnTransformer se alag columns par alag transformers apply hote hain (numerical par num_pipeline, categorical par cat_pipeline). Final preprocessing pipeline 24 features output karti hai: 3 ratio features, 5 log features, 10 cluster similarity features, 5 one-hot category features, aur 1 bacha hua feature (housing_median_age).

Yaad rakho: missing values → impute karo (median safe default); categorical → one-hot (ordinal sirf ordered categories ke liye); scaling → fit sirf training data par; aur sab kuch Pipeline/ColumnTransformer mein daalo taaki reproduce aur tune karna easy ho.

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.utils.validation import check_array, check_is_fitted

class StandardScalerClone(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    def __init__(self, with_mean=True):  # no *args or **kwargs!
        self.with_mean = with_mean

    def fit(self, X, y=None):  # y is required even though we don't use it
        X = check_array(X)  # checks that X is an array with finite float values
        self.mean_ = X.mean(axis=0)
        self.scale_ = X.std(axis=0)
        self.scale_[self.scale_ == 0] = 1  # Avoid division by zero for constant features
        self.n_features_in_ = X.shape[1]  # every estimator stores this in fit()
        return self  # always return self!

    def transform(self, X):
        check_is_fitted(self)  # looks for learned attributes (with trailing _)
        X = check_array(X)
        assert self.n_features_in_ == X.shape[1]
        if self.with_mean:
            X = X - self.mean_
        return X / self.scale_

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

class ClusterSimilarity(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    def __init__(self, n_clusters=10, gamma=1.0, random_state=None):
        self.n_clusters = n_clusters
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(self, X, y=None, sample_weight=None):
        self.kmeans_ = KMeans(self.n_clusters, random_state=self.random_state)
        self.kmeans_.fit(X, sample_weight=sample_weight)
        return self  # always return self!

    def transform(self, X):
        return rbf_kernel(X, self.kmeans_.cluster_centers_, gamma=self.gamma)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, names=None):
        return [f"Cluster {i} similarity" for i in range(self.n_clusters)]

cluster_simil = ClusterSimilarity(n_clusters=10, gamma=1., random_state=42)
similarities = cluster_simil.fit_transform(housing[["latitude", "longitude"]])

similarities[:3].round(2)

housing_prepared_fr.head(2)

def column_ratio(X):
    return X[:, [0]] / X[:, [1]]

def ratio_name(function_transformer, feature_names_in):
    return ["ratio"]  # feature names out

def ratio_pipeline():
    return make_pipeline(
        SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
        FunctionTransformer(column_ratio, feature_names_out=ratio_name),
        StandardScaler())

log_pipeline = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    FunctionTransformer(np.log, feature_names_out="one-to-one"),
    StandardScaler())
cluster_simil = ClusterSimilarity(n_clusters=10, gamma=1., random_state=42)
default_num_pipeline = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
                                     StandardScaler())
preprocessing = ColumnTransformer([
        ("bedrooms", ratio_pipeline(), ["total_bedrooms", "total_rooms"]),
        ("rooms_per_house", ratio_pipeline(), ["total_rooms", "households"]),
        ("people_per_house", ratio_pipeline(), ["population", "households"]),
        ("log", log_pipeline, ["total_bedrooms", "total_rooms", "population",
                               "households", "median_income"]),
        ("geo", cluster_simil, ["latitude", "longitude"]),
        ("cat", cat_pipeline, make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)),
    ],
    remainder=default_num_pipeline)  # one column remaining: housing_median_age

housing_prepared = preprocessing.fit_transform(housing)
housing_prepared.shape

preprocessing.get_feature_names_out()

02.3Chapter 2 · End-to-End Machine Learning Projects

Model Train aur Evaluate Karna

Preprocessing pipeline taiyaar hai — ab model select aur train karne ka time hai. Pehle ek simple linear regression se baseline banao, phir decision tree aur random forest try karo, aur har baar training error par bharosa karne ki jagah cross-validation se evaluate karo.

Linear regression baseline — underfitting

make_pipeline(preprocessing, LinearRegression()) se model banaya aur train kiya. Pehle 5 predictions labels se kaafi alag thi — pehli prediction $200,000 se zyada off thi. Training set par RMSE 68,973 aaya. Median house values zyada districts mein $120,000–$265,000 ke beech hain, to yeh typical error bahut badi hai — model underfit kar raha hai: ya to features mein kaafi information nahi hai, ya model kaafi powerful nahi hai. Fix: zyada powerful model, behtar features, ya model par constraints kam karo. (Score method yahan use nahi hui kyunki woh RMSE ki jagah R² deti hai — R² 1 ke jitna kareeb, utna behtar; hamesha mean predict karne par R² 0 hota hai, usse kharab par negative bhi ho sakta hai.)

Decision tree — training par perfect, asal mein overfit

Decision tree try kiya — yeh complex nonlinear relationships dhoondh sakta hai. Training set par RMSE 0.0 aaya — bilkul perfect! Yeh obviously sach nahi ho sakta — model ne training data ko overfit kar liya hai. Test set ko chhoone ki jagah, training set ke andar hi validation chahiye — isliye k-fold cross-validation: training set ko k folds mein baanto, k baar train aur evaluate karo, har baar ek alag fold validation ke liye. cross_val_score() se 10-fold CV mein decision tree ka mean RMSE 66,573 (std ~1,103) aaya — linear regression (mean 70,003, std 4,182) se thoda hi behtar. Training error 0 aur validation error high = severe overfitting ka proof. Cross-validation ka fayda: performance ka estimate bhi milta hai aur uski precision (standard deviation) bhi.

Random forest — ensemble jeet ta hai

Random forest kai decision trees ko features ke random subsets par train karke unki predictions ka average leta hai — aise multi-model systems ko ensembles kehte hain. Agar underlying models diverse hon to unki errors correlate nahi karti, average karne se errors smooth ho jati hain aur overfitting kam hota hai. 10-fold CV mein random forest ka mean RMSE 47,038 (std ~1,021) — bahut behtar! Par training RMSE ~17,551 abhi bhi bahut kam hai — matlab abhi bhi kaafi overfitting hai. Strategy: pehle kai categories ke models try karo (SVMs, neural network bhi), zyada time hyperparameters tweak karne mein mat lagao — 2–5 promising models shortlist karo, phir unhe fine-tune karo.

Fine-tuning — grid search aur randomized search

Hyperparameters manually fiddle karna tedious hai — GridSearchCV tumhare liye search karta hai: tum hyperparameters aur unki values batao, woh cross-validation se saare combinations evaluate karta hai. Example mein n_clusters (5, 8, 10, 15) aur max_features (4, 6, 8, 10) ke 15 combinations × 3-fold CV = 45 rounds training hui. Best combination mili: n_clusters=15, max_features=6, mean test RMSE 43,590 (default hyperparameters se 47,038 se behtar). Pipeline mein nested hyperparameters ko double underscore se refer karte hain — jaise preprocessing__geo__n_clusters. best_estimator_ se best model milta hai, aur refit=True (default) use poore training set par dobara train karta hai. cv_results_ mein har combination ke scores hote hain.

Jab search space bada ho to RandomizedSearchCV behtar hai — saare combinations try karne ki jagah fixed number of random combinations evaluate karta hai. Fayde: continuous hyperparameters ki kai alag values explore hoti hain; bekaar hyperparameter grid search ko 10x slow kar deta hai, random search ko farq nahi padta; 6 hyperparameters × 10 values = 1,000,000 combinations grid mein, random mein jitne iterations chaho. Distributions bhi de sakte ho — jaise randint(low=3, high=50). HalvingRandomSearchCV aur HalvingGridSearchCV aur efficient hain: pehle round mein kai candidates ko kam resources (chhota training set) par evaluate karo, sirf best ko agle round mein zyada resources do. Ensemble methods bhi try karo — best models ko combine karna aksar best individual model se behtar hota hai.

Best model aur uski errors analyze karo

Random forest feature_importances_ batata hai kaunsa attribute kitna important hai: sabse important log__median_income (~0.19), phir cat__ocean_proximity_INLAND (~0.07), bedrooms__ratio (~0.066), rooms_per_house__ratio (~0.054). Kam useful features drop karke try kar sakte ho — SelectFromModel transformer yeh automatically karta hai. Specific errors ko bhi dekho: extra features add karo, uninformative features hatao, outliers clean karo. Aur fairness check karo — model sirf average par acha na ho, balki rural/urban, rich/poor, north/south, har category ke districts par acha ho. Agar kisi category par kharab perform karta hai to deploy mat karo jab tak issue resolve na ho.

Test set par final evaluation

Final model ko test set par evaluate karo: final RMSE 41,448 aaya. Sirf point estimate kaafi nahi hota — 95% confidence interval bhi nikalo (bootstrap se): 39,515 se 43,706. Dhyaan: bahut hyperparameter tuning ke baad performance validation se thodi kharab hoti hai, kyunki system validation data ke liye fine-tune ho jata hai — test set par numbers ache dikhane ke liye hyperparameters tweak karne ki temptation se bacho, woh improvements naye data par generalize nahi karengi. Solution present karte waqt concise reports banao, key insights visualize karo, audience ke hisaab se message tailor karo ("median income housing prices ka number one predictor hai" jaise impactful statements), assumptions aur limitations batao, aur results reproducible rakho — code accessible rakho, README likho, requirements.txt ya environment file do, random seeds set karo.

Yaad rakho: training error 0 matlab perfect model nahi, overfitting hai. Hamesha cross-validation se evaluate karo, phir grid/random search se fine-tune karo, aur test set sirf aakhir mein ek baar use karo.

02.4Chapter 2 · End-to-End Machine Learning Projects

Launch, Monitor aur Maintain Karna

Model approve ho gaya — ab production ki baari hai. Launch karna sirf model save karke upload karna nahi hai; monitoring, retraining, input quality check aur rollback plan bhi chahiye. Yeh kaam aksar model banane se bhi zyada bada hota hai — is field ko MLOps kehte hain.

Model deploy karna

Sabse basic tareeka: best model ko joblib.dump(final_model, "my_california_housing_model.pkl") se save karo, file ko production environment mein transfer karo, aur joblib.load() se load karke predict() karo. Load karne se pehle woh saare custom classes aur functions import karne honge jin par model depend karta hai — isliye code bhi production mein transfer karna padta hai. Har experiment kiya hua model save karna acha idea hai — taaki kisi bhi model par wapas ja sako, scores aur predictions compare kar sako.

Doosre options: model ko ek dedicated web service mein wrap karo jise web application REST API se query kare — isse model ko upgrade karna easy hota hai bina main application roke, scaling easy hoti hai (load balancing ke saath kai services), aur web application kisi bhi programming language mein ho sakti hai. Ya model ko cloud par deploy karo — jaise file ko cloud storage par upload karke ek managed service mein model version banao, jo load balancing aur scaling khud handle kare aur JSON requests par JSON predictions de.

Monitoring — performance girne par alert

Deploy karne ke baad monitoring code likho jo live performance ko regular intervals par check kare aur girne par alert trigger kare. Performance bahut jaldi gir sakti hai (koi component toot gaya) ya bahut slowly decay kar sakti hai — slowly decay notice karna mushkil hota hai, aur iska common reason hai data drift: model pichhle saal ke data par train hua tha, aaj ke data par fit nahi baithta. Performance infer karne ke tareeke: downstream metrics (jaise recommender system mein recommended products ki daily sales girna), ya human raters — model ke classify kiye hue pictures ka sample (khaas taur par jin par model sure nahi tha) experts ya crowdsourcing workers ko check karne ke liye bhejo. Users khud bhi raters ho sakte hain — surveys ya repurposed captchas ke through.

Retraining automate karo aur backups rakho

  • Fresh data regularly collect karo aur label karo (human raters se).
  • Training aur hyperparameter fine-tuning automate karo — script roz ya hafte mein ek baar khud chal sakti hai.
  • Naye aur purane model ko updated test set par compare karo — performance giri nahi ho to hi deploy karo; giri ho to investigate karo. Test set ke alag-alag subsets (poor/rich, rural/urban districts) par bhi check karo.
  • Input data quality monitor karo — kabhi performance isliye girti hai kyunki input signal kharab hai (jaise malfunctioning sensor random values bhej raha ho, ya kisi aur team ka output stale ho gaya ho). Alert trigger karo agar missing features badhne lagein, mean ya standard deviation training set se bahut drift kare, ya categorical feature mein nayi categories aane lagein.
  • Har model ka backup rakho taaki kharab model se turant purane model par rollback kar sako, aur naye models ko purane se compare kar sako. Datasets ke har version ka backup bhi rakho — taaki corrupted dataset se wapas ja sako aur kisi bhi model ko kisi bhi purane dataset par evaluate kar sako.
Yaad rakho: deployment end nahi hai, shuruaat hai. Monitoring system (human raters ke saath ya bina), failure processes, automated retraining aur backups — yeh sab lagana aksar model train karne se zyada kaam hota hai. Lekin ek baar infrastructure ban gaya, to idea se production tak jana bahut fast ho jata hai.

from sklearn.base import MetaEstimatorMixin, clone
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

class FeatureFromRegressor(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin, MetaEstimatorMixin):
    def __init__(self, regressor, target_features):
        self.regressor = regressor
        self.target_features = target_features

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        if hasattr(X, "columns"):
            self.feature_names_in_ = list(X.columns)
            X_df = X
        else:
            X_df = pd.DataFrame(X)
        
        self.input_features_ = [c for c in X_df.columns
                                if c not in self.target_features]
        self.regressor_ = clone(self.regressor)
        self.regressor_.fit(X_df[self.input_features_],
                            X_df[self.target_features])
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        columns = X.columns if hasattr(X, "columns") else None
        X_df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=columns)
        preds = self.regressor_.predict(X_df[self.input_features_])
        if preds.ndim == 1:
            preds = preds.reshape(-1, 1)
        extra_columns = [f"pred_{t}" for t in self.target_features]
        preds_df = pd.DataFrame(preds, columns=extra_columns, index=X_df.index)
        return pd.concat([X_df, preds_df], axis=1)
    
    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        extra_columns = [f"pred_{t}" for t in self.target_features]
        return self.feature_names_in_ + extra_columns

    def fit_transform(self, X, y=None):
        self.fit(X, y)
        X_df = pd.DataFrame(X)
        # Held-out predictions prevent each district from predicting itself.
        preds = cross_val_predict(self.regressor, X_df[self.input_features_],
                                  X_df[self.target_features], cv=5)
        extra_columns = [f"pred_{t}" for t in self.target_features]
        preds_df = pd.DataFrame(preds, columns=extra_columns, index=X_df.index)
        return pd.concat([X_df, preds_df], axis=1)

import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.utils.validation import check_is_fitted, validate_data

class StandardScalerClone(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def __init__(self, with_mean=True):  # no *args or **kwargs!
        self.with_mean = with_mean

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = validate_data(self, X, ensure_2d=True)
        self.n_features_in_ = X.shape[1]
        if self.with_mean:
            self.mean_ = np.mean(X, axis=0)
        self.scale_ = np.std(X, axis=0, ddof=0)
        self.scale_[self.scale_ == 0] = 1  # Avoid division by zero
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        check_is_fitted(self)
        X = validate_data(self, X, ensure_2d=True, reset=False)
        if self.with_mean:
            X = X - self.mean_
        return X / self.scale_

    def inverse_transform(self, X):
        check_is_fitted(self)
        X = validate_data(self, X, ensure_2d=True, reset=False)
        X = X * self.scale_
        if self.with_mean:
            X = X + self.mean_
        return X

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        if input_features is None:
            return getattr(self, "feature_names_in_",
                           [f"x{i}" for i in range(self.n_features_in_)])
        else:
            if len(input_features) != self.n_features_in_:
                raise ValueError("Invalid number of features")
            if hasattr(self, "feature_names_in_") and not np.all(
                self.feature_names_in_ == input_features
            ):
                raise ValueError("input_features ≠ feature_names_in_")
            return input_features

from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import check_estimator

check_estimator(StandardScalerClone())

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
X = rng.random((1000, 3))

scaler = StandardScalerClone()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

assert np.allclose(X_scaled, (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0))

scaler = StandardScalerClone(with_mean=False)
X_scaled_uncentered = scaler.fit_transform(X)

assert np.allclose(X_scaled_uncentered, X / X.std(axis=0))

scaler = StandardScalerClone()
X_back = scaler.inverse_transform(scaler.fit_transform(X))

assert np.allclose(X, X_back)

assert np.all(scaler.get_feature_names_out() == ["x0", "x1", "x2"])
assert np.all(scaler.get_feature_names_out(["a", "b", "c"]) == ["a", "b", "c"])

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": rng.random(100), "b": rng.random(100)})
scaler = StandardScalerClone()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(df)

assert np.all(scaler.feature_names_in_ == ["a", "b"])
assert np.all(scaler.get_feature_names_out() == ["a", "b"])

03Chapter 3 · Classification

Classification

Chapter 1 mein bataya tha ki supervised learning ke do sabse common tasks hain — regression (values predict karna) aur classification (classes predict karna). Chapter 2 mein regression kiya (housing prices); ab classification ki baari hai, MNIST dataset par — handwritten digits ki images.

MNIST dataset — ML ka "hello world"

MNIST mein 70,000 chhoti images hain handwritten digits ki, har image par us digit ka label hai. Har image 28×28 pixels ki hai, isliye har instance mein 784 features hain — har feature ek pixel ki intensity hai, 0 (white) se 255 (black). Dataset fetch_openml('mnist_784', as_frame=False) se milta hai. Scikit-Learn ke datasets package mein teen types ke functions hain: fetch_* (real datasets download karna), load_* (chhote toy datasets jo Scikit-Learn ke saath bundled hain), aur make_* (tests ke liye fake datasets generate karna). MNIST pehle se split hai: pehle 60,000 images training set, aakhri 10,000 test set. Training set pehle se shuffled hai — yeh acha hai kyunki cross-validation folds similar honge aur kuch algorithms ko similar instances ek ke baad ek milne par problem hoti hai.

Binary classifier train karna — 5-detector

Problem simplify karte hain: sirf digit 5 pehchanna hai — yeh binary classifier hai (sirf do classes: 5 aur non-5). Targets banaye: y_train_5 = (y_train == '5'). Phir SGDClassifier (stochastic gradient descent classifier) train kiya — yeh bahut bade datasets efficiently handle karta hai kyunki woh training instances ko ek-ek karke process karta hai, aur online learning ke liye bhi suited hai. Ek example image par predict() ne sahi jawab diya: True (yeh 5 hai). Ab performance evaluate karte hain.

Accuracy dhokha de sakti hai

3-fold cross-validation mein SGD classifier ki accuracy 95% se zyada aayi — amazing lagta hai, par ruko. Ek dummy classifier jo har image ko sabse frequent class (non-5) mein daale, uski accuracy bhi 90% se zyada hai — kyunki sirf lagbhag 10% images hi 5 hain. Hamesha guess karo "5 nahi hai" to 90% baar sahi ho jaoge! Isliye accuracy generally classifiers ke liye preferred performance measure nahi hai, khaas taur par skewed datasets mein jahan kuch classes bahut zyada frequent hon. Behtar tareeka hai confusion matrix dekhna — jo agle section mein hai.

Yaad rakho: MNIST 70,000 images, 784 features (28×28 pixels), 60,000 train + 10,000 test. Accuracy akele kaafi nahi — hamesha poocho ki classes balanced hain ya skewed.

03.1Chapter 3 · Classification

Performance Measure Karna — Accuracy, Confusion Matrix, Precision-Recall

Classifier evaluate karna regressor evaluate karne se zyada tricky hai — isliye is chapter ka bada hissa performance measures par hai. Cross-validation, confusion matrix, precision, recall aur F1 score — sab ek saath samjho.

Cross-validation se accuracy — aur uski limit

cross_val_score(sgd_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3, scoring="accuracy") se teen folds mein accuracy mili: 0.95035, 0.96035, 0.9604 — 95% se zyada. Par dummy classifier (hamesha non-5 predict karo) ki bhi accuracy 0.90965 hai. Khud cross-validation implement karni ho to StratifiedKFold use karo — yeh stratified sampling se folds banata hai jinme har class ka representative ratio ho; har iteration mein classifier ka clone banao, training folds par train karo, test fold par predict karo, aur correct predictions ka ratio nikalo.

Confusion matrix — chaar numbers mein poori kahani

Confusion matrix gin-ti karti hai ki class A ke instances ko class B ke roop mein kitni baar classify kiya gaya. cross_val_predict() se har instance ke liye clean (out-of-sample) predictions lo — model ne woh data training mein kabhi dekha nahi — phir confusion_matrix(y_train_5, y_train_pred) se matrix banao. 5-detector ki matrix: [[53892, 687], [1891, 3530]]. Rows actual class hain, columns predicted class: true negatives 53,892 (non-5 sahi pehchane), false positives 687 (non-5 ko 5 bola — type I error), false negatives 1,891 (5 ko non-5 bola — type II error), true positives 3,530 (5 sahi pehchane). Perfect classifier ki matrix mein sirf main diagonal par nonzero values hoti.

Precision, recall aur F1 score

  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — jab classifier "positive" bolta hai, to kitni baar sahi hota hai. Yahan 3530 / (687 + 3530) = 0.837 — 83.7%.
  • Recall (sensitivity ya true positive rate, TPR) = TP / (TP + FN) — positive instances mein se kitne detect hue. Yahan 3530 / (1891 + 3530) = 0.651 — sirf 65.1% 5s detect hue.
  • F1 score = precision aur recall ka harmonic mean — 2 × (precision × recall) / (precision + recall) — yahan 0.733. Harmonic mean low values ko zyada weight deta hai, isliye F1 tabhi high hota hai jab precision aur recall dono high hon.

Kabhi precision zyada important hoti hai (jaise kids-safe videos detect karna — ek bhi bura video nahi aana chahiye, recall kam chalega), kabhi recall (jaise shoplifters ya medical diagnosis — kuch miss nahi hona chahiye, false alarms chalenge). Dono ek saath nahi badh sakte — yeh precision/recall trade-off hai.

Threshold se trade-off control karna

SGD classifier har instance ke liye ek score compute karta hai (decision_function() se) — score threshold se zyada ho to positive class, warna negative. Threshold badhao to precision badhti hai, recall girti hai; threshold ghatao to ulta. Example: threshold 0 par ek 5 ki image detect hoti hai, threshold 3,000 par miss ho jati hai. precision_recall_curve() se har possible threshold ke liye precision aur recall nikalo aur plot karo. 90% precision chahiye to threshold lagbhag 3,370 chahiye — precision 0.90, recall 0.48. Kisi ne kaha "99% precision chahiye" to pehla sawaal poocho: "kis recall par?" Scikit-Learn 1.5 se FixedThresholdClassifier (manual threshold) aur TunedThresholdClassifierCV (cross-validation se optimal threshold — default balanced accuracy maximize karta hai, jo har class ke recall ka average hai) bhi available hain.

Yaad rakho: accuracy skewed data mein dhokha deti hai. Confusion matrix dekho, phir precision aur recall — aur apne project ke hisaab se decide karo kiski zyada zaroorat hai, threshold se trade-off set karo.

03.2Chapter 3 · Classification

Multiclass, Multilabel aur Multioutput Classification

Ab tak har instance sirf ek class mein jata tha, aur sirf do classes thi. Real duniya mein aisa nahi hota — kabhi 10 classes hoti hain, kabhi ek instance par multiple labels, kabhi har label ke multiple values. Yeh section teeno types cover karta hai.

Multiclass — one-vs-rest aur one-vs-one

Multiclass classifiers (multinomial) do se zyada classes distinguish karte hain. Kuch classifiers (jaise LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier) multiple classes natively handle karte hain; kuch strictly binary hote hain (jaise SGDClassifier, SVC). Binary classifiers se multiclass karne ke do strategies: one-versus-the-rest (OvR / OvA) — har class ke liye ek binary classifier train karo (10 digits ke liye 10 classifiers), phir jis classifier ka decision score sabse zyada, woh class chuno. One-versus-one (OvO) — har pair ke liye ek binary classifier (N classes ke liye N×(N−1)/2 classifiers — MNIST ke liye 45), phir image ko sabse zyada duels jeetne wali class do. OvO ka fayda: har classifier sirf do classes wale chhote training set par train hota hai — isliye slow algorithms (jaise SVM) ke liye OvO preferred hai; baaki ke liye OvR. Scikit-Learn khud detect karke OvR ya OvO chunta hai. SVC ko pehle 2,000 images par train kiya gaya (zyada par bahut slow hota) — usne 45 classifiers train kiye aur ek 5 ki image sahi classify ki. OneVsOneClassifier aur OneVsRestClassifier se force bhi kar sakte ho. SGD multiclass mein OvR use karta hai — uski accuracy ~87% aayi, aur inputs scale karne par 89% se zyada ho gayi.

ROC curve aur AUC — classifier compare karna

ROC curve true positive rate (recall) ko false positive rate (FPR) ke against plot karti hai. FPR = galat tareeke se positive classify kiye gaye negative instances ka ratio = 1 − specificity (true negative rate). Random classifier ki ROC curve diagonal hoti hai; acha classifier top-left corner ke kareeb rehta hai. Area under the curve (AUC) se classifiers compare karte hain: perfect classifier ka ROC AUC 1, random ka 0.5. SGD 5-detector ka ROC AUC 0.960 aaya. Random forest ka ROC AUC 0.998 aur F1 0.927 — precision lagbhag 99.0% aur recall 87.3%. Rule of thumb: jab positive class rare ho ya false positives zyada important hon, to PR curve prefer karo; warna ROC curve. ROC curve dekhkar classifier bahut acha lag sakta hai jab positives kam hon — PR curve asli picture dikhati hai. Ek warning: predict_proba() ki estimated probabilities actual probabilities nahi hoti — model overconfident ya underconfident ho sakta hai; CalibratedClassifierCV se calibrate kar sakte ho, jo medical diagnosis ya fraud detection jaise cases mein important hai.

Multilabel — ek instance, multiple tags

Kabhi ek instance par multiple binary tags lagte hain — jaise ek photo mein kai log hon to face-recognition classifier har pehchane gaye shakhs ke liye ek tag de. Example: har digit ke liye do labels — kya digit bada hai (7, 8, 9) aur kya woh odd hai. KNeighborsClassifier multilabel support karta hai (sab nahi karte) — digit 5 ke liye prediction [False, True] aayi — sahi hai (5 bada nahi, odd hai). Evaluate karne ka ek tareeka: har label ka F1 score nikalo aur average karo — average="macro" se 0.976 aaya (sab labels equally important mane). Agar kisi label ke zyada instances hon to average="weighted" se support ke hisaab se weight do. Jo classifier multilabel natively support nahi karta (jaise SVC), uske liye har label par ek model train karo — par isse labels ke beech dependencies miss ho jati hain (bada digit odd hone ki probability double hoti hai). Solution: ClassifierChain — models ko chain mein organize karo, har model ko input features + pehle wale models ki predictions milti hain. cv set karne par chain cross-validation se clean out-of-sample predictions use karta hai.

Multioutput — har label ke multiple values

Multioutput (multiclass) classification multilabel ka generalization hai — har label ke do se zyada possible values ho sakte hain. Example: noisy digit image ko clean karna — input noisy image, output clean image (har pixel ki intensity 0–255). Output multilabel hai (har pixel ek label) aur har label multiclass hai (pixel intensity ke kai values). Training data banane ke liye MNIST images mein random noise (0–100) add kiya gaya, targets original images rakhe gaye. KNeighborsClassifier train karke noisy image clean ki gayi — result target ke bahut kareeb aaya. Note: classification aur regression ke beech ki line yahan blurry hai — pixel intensity predict karna regression jaisa bhi lag sakta hai, aur multioutput systems sirf classification tak limited nahi hain.

Yaad rakho: multiclass = OvR (10 classifiers) ya OvO (45 classifiers); multilabel = multiple binary tags, evaluate macro ya weighted F1 se; multioutput = har label ke multiple values, jaise image denoising.
Poora code dekho — ROC curve (Notebook 03, Ch 3)

03.3Chapter 3 · Classification

Error Analysis aur ROC Curves

Model train karna kaafi nahi — uski errors analyze karna bhi zaroori hai. Confusion matrix ko plot karke, errors ko normalize karke, aur galat classify hui images ko dekhkar pata chalta hai model kahan fail ho raha hai aur use kaise improve karein.

Confusion matrix plot karna aur normalize karna

10 classes ki confusion matrix mein bahut numbers hote hain — colored diagram easy hota hai: ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_train, y_train_pred) se. Zyada images main diagonal par hain (sahi classify hui). Par row 5, column 5 ka cell thoda dark hai — ya to 5s par zyada errors hain, ya 5s kam hain. Isliye matrix ko normalize karo: har value ko us row ke total se divide karo (normalize="true", values_format=".0%"). Ab saaf dikhta hai: sirf 82% 5s sahi classify hue; sabse common error — 10% 5s ko 8 classify kiya gaya. Par sirf 2% 8s ko 5 classify kiya gaya — confusion matrices generally symmetrical nahi hoti!

Sirf errors par focus karna

Errors ko highlight karne ke liye correct predictions ko zero weight do (sample_weight=(y_train_pred != y_train)). Ab column 8 bahut bright hai — lagbhag har class ki images galat tareeke se 8 classify ho rahi hain. Percentages interpret karte waqt careful raho: 7s wali row mein 9s wale column mein 36% ka matlab yeh nahi ki 36% 7s ko 9 bola gaya — matlab hai ki 7s par hui errors mein se 36% errors 9 ke roop mein thi; asal mein sirf 3% 7s ko 9 classify kiya gaya tha. Column se normalize karne par (normalize="pred") pata chalta hai ki misclassified 7s mein se 56% asal mein 9s the. Insights: false 8s kam karne par focus karo — jaise 8 jaisi dikhne wali digits ka zyada training data lao, naye features engineer karo (jaise closed loops ginna — 8 mein do, 6 mein ek, 5 mein zero), ya images preprocess karo taaki patterns (jaise closed loops) zyada clear hon.

Individual errors dekhna aur data augmentation

3s aur 5s ki misclassified images ko confusion-matrix style mein plot karke dekho: kuch digits itne kharab likhe hain ki human bhi mushkil se classify kar paye, par zyada misclassified images humein obvious errors lagti hain. Wajah: SGDClassifier ek linear model hai — har pixel ko har class ke liye ek weight deta hai, aur nayi image dekhkar weighted pixel intensities ka sum karke score nikalta hai. 3 aur 5 mein sirf kuch pixels ka farq hai, isliye model confuse hota hai. 3 aur 5 ka main farq hai woh chhoti line jo top line ko bottom arc se jodti hai — junction thoda left shift ho to 3, 5 lag sakta hai. Matlab classifier image shifting aur rotation ke liye sensitive hai. Fix: images ko center aur rotate karke preprocess karo (mushkil), ya training set ko shifted/rotated variants se bada karo — isse data augmentation kehte hain, jo model ko variations ke prati tolerant banata hai.

Yaad rakho: error analysis mein pehle confusion matrix normalize karo (row se, phir column se), phir sirf errors dikhao, phir individual galat images dekho. Har error ek hint hai — zyada data, behtar features, ya data augmentation mein se kya chahiye.

from scipy.ndimage import shift

def shift_image(image, dx, dy):
    image = image.reshape((28, 28))
    shifted_image = shift(image, [dy, dx], cval=0, mode="constant")
    return shifted_image.reshape([-1])

def load_titanic_data():

import tarfile

def fetch_spam_data():
    spam_root = "http://spamassassin.apache.org/old/publiccorpus/"
    ham_url = spam_root + "20030228_easy_ham.tar.bz2"
    spam_url = spam_root + "20030228_spam.tar.bz2"

    spam_path = Path() / "datasets" / "spam"
    spam_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for dir_name, tar_name, url in (("easy_ham", "ham", ham_url),
                                    ("spam", "spam", spam_url)):
        if not (spam_path / dir_name).is_dir():
            path = (spam_path / tar_name).with_suffix(".tar.bz2")
            print("Downloading", path)
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, path)
            tar_bz2_file = tarfile.open(path)
            tar_bz2_file.extractall(path=spam_path, filter="data")
            tar_bz2_file.close()
    return [spam_path / dir_name for dir_name in ("easy_ham", "spam")]

import email
import email.policy

def load_email(filepath):
    with open(filepath, "rb") as f:
        return email.parser.BytesParser(policy=email.policy.default).parse(f)

ham_emails = [load_email(filepath) for filepath in ham_filenames]

def get_email_structure(email):
    if isinstance(email, str):
        return email
    payload = email.get_payload()
    if isinstance(payload, list):
        multipart = ", ".join([get_email_structure(sub_email)
                               for sub_email in payload])
        return f"multipart({multipart})"
    else:
        return email.get_content_type()

from collections import Counter

def structures_counter(emails):
    structures = Counter()
    for email in emails:
        structure = get_email_structure(email)
        structures[structure] += 1
    return structures

import re
from html import unescape

def html_to_plain_text(html):
    text = re.sub(r'<head.*?>.*?</head>', '', html, flags=re.M | re.S | re.I)
    text = re.sub(r'<a\s.*?>', ' HYPERLINK ', text, flags=re.M | re.S | re.I)
    text = re.sub(r'<.*?>', '', text, flags=re.M | re.S)
    text = re.sub(r'(\s*\n)+', '\n', text, flags=re.M | re.S)
    return unescape(text)

html_spam_emails = [email for email in X_train[y_train==1]
                    if get_email_structure(email) == "text/html"]
